result:
There's a Portuguese word, *saudade*, that names the ache for something absent—not just missing a person, but missing a version of the world that no longer exists, or perhaps never did. English has no equivalent. We say "I miss you" and leave it there, flattened, like pressing a flower until all its dimension is gone.

Languages are full of these small locked doors. The Japanese *komorebi* describes sunlight filtering through leaves—a whole phenomenon compressed into four syllables. The German *Fernweh* is homesickness for places you've never been, a reverse nostalgia. The Yaghan word *mamihlapinatapai* captures the look between two people who both want to start something but neither will move first.

What I love about these words is what they reveal: that experience outruns vocabulary everywhere, and every culture has noticed different gaps. Somewhere, centuries ago, a person felt sunlight through leaves so specifically that they needed a name for it, and enough others agreed that the word survived.

It makes me wonder what we're all feeling right now that has no name yet. Some emotion unique to this century—the strange grief of a dying group chat, the loneliness of being reachable at all times. Future languages will carve words for these, probably, and speakers will assume everyone always felt this way.

But every word was invented once, by someone standing in a particular light, needing to say what it was like. That's the whole history of language, really—one person after another, reaching.
